1	# Versioning
2	
3	How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
4	suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
5	copied **verbatim**, with
6	[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
7	conditional rather than per-project edits.
8	
9	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
10	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
11	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
12	
13	## Terms
14	
15	Three names, used as defined here across
16	[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
17	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:
18	
19	- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
20	  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
21	  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
22	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
23	  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
24	  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
25	- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
26	  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
27	  artifact derives from it.
28	- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.
29	
30	## A stamp, not a name
31	
32	The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
33	named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
34	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
35	suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
36	inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.
37	
38	## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides
39	
40	Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
41	touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**
42	
43	- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
44	  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
45	  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
46	  presentation, docs, notes.
47	- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
48	  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
49	- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
50	  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).
51	
52	**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
53	thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.
54	
55	## Grammar and storage
56	
57	One spelling everywhere the version is written:
58	
59	```
60	<public>[-<suffix>]
61	```
62	
63	- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
64	- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
65	  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
66	- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
67	  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
68	  version storable in every medium below.
69	- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
70	  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a leading `v`;
71	  Cargo rejects one.)
72	
73	Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
74	
75	- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
76	  valid at any dot depth.
77	- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
78	  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
79	- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
80	  adds its case to
81	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
82	
83	Two reservations keep the remap sound:
84	
85	- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
86	  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out); PEP 440 sorts the
87	  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
88	  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
89	  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
90	- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
91	  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
92	  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.
93	
94	**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
95	multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
96	2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
97	`+` are all invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but
98	silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
99	every medium accepts.
100	
101	## Recording the version-of-record
102	
103	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
104	the case that fits your medium:
105	
106	- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
107	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
108	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
109	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
110	    ...). Add the case as needed
111	- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
112	  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
113	  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
114	    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
115	- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
116	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
117	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
118	- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
119	  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
120	  per-commit preference.
121	
122	## Dev artifact name
123	
124	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
125	active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
126	clobbers the binary consumers are running:
127	
128	- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
129	  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
130	  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
131	- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
132	  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
133	  install dir with stale binaries.
134	- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
135	  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
136	  flow's install.
137	
138	Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
139	its `custom.md` layer.
140	
141	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
142	
143	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
144	running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.
145	
146	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
147	  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
148	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
149	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
150	  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
151	  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).
152	
153	## Suffix scheme
154	
155	The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
156	each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.
157	
158	This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
159	not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
160	neither a number nor a version (see
161	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
162	prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
163	commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
164	nothing dereferences one.
165	
166	- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
167	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
168	- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
169	
170	**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
171	and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
172	Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
173	without renumbering siblings.
174	
175	Disambiguation:
176	
177	- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
178	- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
179	
180	**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
181	
182	- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
183	- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
184	- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
185	- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle
186	
187	Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
188	step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
189	above, every commit carries a distinct version.

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
conditional rather than per-project edits.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
  artifact derives from it.
- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.

## A stamp, not a name

The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.

## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides

Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**

- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
  presentation, docs, notes.
- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).

**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.

## Grammar and storage

One spelling everywhere the version is written:

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
  version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a leading `v`;
  Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
  valid at any dot depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
  adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out); PEP 440 sorts the
  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.

**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
`+` are all invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but
silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
the case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
    ...). Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
  per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
its `custom.md` layer.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
above, every commit carries a distinct version.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
8	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
14	or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
15	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
16	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
17	fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
18	they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
19	naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
20	[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
21	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
22	
23	Surfaces that use this shape:
24	
25	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
26	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
27	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
28	  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
29	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
30	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
31	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
32	  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
33	  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
34	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).
35	
36	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
37	
38	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, a problem
39	  statement then a solution statement, both broad. What is specific to a commit:
40	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
41	    meets first and it answers the problem
42	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
43	    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
44	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
45	    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
46	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
47	    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
48	    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
49	    here
50	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
51	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
52	  list. See
53	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
54	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
55	
56	### Line widths
57	
58	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
59	than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
60	2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
61	
62	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
63	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
64	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
65	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
66	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
67	  convention here 2026-08-09; published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
68	
69	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
70	when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
71	imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
72	a literal report row, indented code in a comment).
73	
74	### Problem-first shape
75	
76	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
77	form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
78	
79	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
80	  what follows it.
81	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
82	  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in
83	  [Bullet content differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
84	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
85	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See
86	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
87	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
88	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is
89	    picked up into a cycle.
90	
91	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A
92	cycle writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's
93	commit body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a
94	commit body's is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule
95	here said a plan was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle
96	unable to say at its opening what it intended to do.
97	
98	### Semicolons
99	
100	A semicolon earns its place only between equals: two parallel claims of the same weight, where
101	the contrast is the point ("The diff empties; the history keeps the record"). Everything else
102	that reaches for one is a structure decision not yet made. Make the decision:
103	
104	- **Item plus detail** (`claim; elaboration`): a detail worth keeping gets its own sentence, or
105	  its own sub-bullet where a reader skimming the list will actually notice it. A mere
106	  continuation of the thought takes a comma with a conjunction.
107	- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a bullet): break the clauses into sub-bullets so
108	  the structure shows.
109	- **Legitimate besides the antithesis**: a semicolon separating list items that themselves
110	  contain commas; and semicolons inside code spans, which are syntax, not prose.
111	
112	Running prose is held to the same test, just less strictly: a sentence-join in an intro
113	paragraph is fine when both halves would stand as sentences and neither is a detail of the
114	other.
115	
116	### Typeable punctuation only
117	
118	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
119	*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
120	below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
121	Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
122	paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
123	Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on
124	every read, so a soft rule accumulates them.
125	
126	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
127	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
128	
129	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
130	  sub-bullets.
131	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
132	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
133	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
134	  go.
135	
136	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
137	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
138	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
139	commit.
140	
141	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
142	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
143	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
144	prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
145	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
146	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
147	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
148	
149	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
150	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
151	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
152	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
153	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
154	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
155	
156	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
157	
158	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
159	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
160	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
161	They differ in the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
162	problem-then-solution, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
163	above). The shared template:
164	
165	```
166	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
167	<optional prose intro>
168	  - <optional item>
169	    <optional prose intro>
170	      - <optional sub-item>
171	      ...
172	```
173	
174	The three surfaces apply it as:
175	
176	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is the bare title plus a `(current)` /
177	  `(done)` marker, and its position in the list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is
178	  the close-out and its text says so. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
179	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no prefix, since the `##` header *is* the
180	  bare title. The as-built ladder is the first content under it (see
181	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
182	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose
183	  (see [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)).
184	
185	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
186	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim. Pick the commit title first and
187	reuse it.
188	
189	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
190	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
191	section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
192	with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
193	
194	**Cycle bookend titles**: the opening commit's title is the close-out title plus " opening",
195	same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` / `feat: dynamic warmup`), so one
196	`git log --grep "<close-out title>"` returns exactly the pair that brackets the cycle. The
197	type repeats the close-out's even though an opening is mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes
198	make the pair scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.
199	
200	### Steps are named, not numbered
201	
202	A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung, a chores as-built rung, a `## Done`
203	entry, or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a rung's place in the list already *is* its place in
204	the ladder, so a number beside it would restate the position and then have to be maintained.
205	
206	- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
207	  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
208	- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable in the two places a
209	  title is resolved: within its own cycle, so a ladder rung names one step, and within its chores
210	  file, since a `##` header is also an anchor and a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first
211	  one. Across the repo's history a title may repeat.
212	- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and
213	  nothing else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder
214	  come along. See
215	  [Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
216	- **`## Todo` ranks are the exception that stays numbered**, because a priority list has an order
217	  worth reading off (see [Todo format](notes.md#todo-format)). Those numbers are positional too,
218	  and are equally never used as references.
219	
220	### Versions live in the version-of-record only
221	
222	No version appears in durable prose: not in an in-flight ladder rung, a chores header, a commit
223	title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only written home (see
224	[versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from that file at that
225	commit.
226	
227	**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
228	for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
229	one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
230	residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.
231	
232	**Two surfaces record a version rather than name a step.** Both record a *commit*, never a step,
233	which is what keeps them outside the rule rather than exceptions to it:
234	
235	- **A chores as-built rung** records a version alongside that commit's SHA once the commit is on
236	  a permanent branch. The pair decodes an old `-V` banner or a pasted report. It obeys the SHA's
237	  timing exactly, so a rung on an unlanded branch carries neither (see
238	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
239	- **A `## Done` entry**, in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`, carries the close-out's version ahead of
240	  its title (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Here the version is the search
241	  key: the question a reader arrives with is "what shipped in 0.42.0", and with no version
242	  written anywhere in the Done list that question has no answer.
243	
244	The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
245	because a commit cannot record its own SHA; a Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
246	is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
247	unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
248	([Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)), and a renumber of
249	published versions rewrites it in the same sweep as the rungs.
250	
251	**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
252	opening"). Writing *about* versioning is unaffected: a version named as a specimen, whether in the
253	scheme's own notation, a decoder table, or a narrative about a renumber, is a use of the word
254	rather than an identifier for a step, the same distinction
255	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws between naming a character and using
256	one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.
257	
258	## Pinned files name no project
259	
260	A pinned agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names a member project, a member's
261	history, or a member's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every member
262	shares and stay. What is barred is a member repo appearing in universal text.
263	
264	**Why:** pinned text is copied to every member, so a project narration reads as the reader's own
265	history ("This project adopted the convention on <date>" arrives in repos that adopted it on a
266	different date or never). And the citation goes stale the moment the named project retires its
267	records, while the rule outlives it.
268	
269	**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file; leave the evidence trail
270	in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
271	that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
272	specimen in
273	the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
274	reference, per the same distinction
275	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
276	draws.
277	
278	## Speculation marker
279	
280	Durable text the bot writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
281	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
282	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
283	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
284	
285	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
286	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
287	worth keeping visible in the written record.
288	
289	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
290	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
291	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
292	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
293	on hand.
294	
295	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
296	
297	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
298	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
299	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
300	
301	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
302	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
303	
304	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
305	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
306	synopsis.

# Prose and durable text

How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
comments, chores sections).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, a problem
  statement then a solution statement, both broad. What is specific to a commit:
  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
    meets first and it answers the problem
  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
    here
- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
  list. See
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Line widths

Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.

- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
  convention here 2026-08-09; published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.

The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
a literal report row, indented code in a comment).

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
  what follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in
  [Bullet content differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See
    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is
    picked up into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A
cycle writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's
commit body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a
commit body's is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule
here said a plan was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle
unable to say at its opening what it intended to do.

### Semicolons

A semicolon earns its place only between equals: two parallel claims of the same weight, where
the contrast is the point ("The diff empties; the history keeps the record"). Everything else
that reaches for one is a structure decision not yet made. Make the decision:

- **Item plus detail** (`claim; elaboration`): a detail worth keeping gets its own sentence, or
  its own sub-bullet where a reader skimming the list will actually notice it. A mere
  continuation of the thought takes a comma with a conjunction.
- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a bullet): break the clauses into sub-bullets so
  the structure shows.
- **Legitimate besides the antithesis**: a semicolon separating list items that themselves
  contain commas; and semicolons inside code spans, which are syntax, not prose.

Running prose is held to the same test, just less strictly: a sentence-join in an intro
paragraph is fine when both halves would stand as sentences and neither is a detail of the
other.

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on
every read, so a soft rule accumulates them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
  sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
  go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
They differ in the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
problem-then-solution, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
above). The shared template:

```
<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is the bare title plus a `(current)` /
  `(done)` marker, and its position in the list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is
  the close-out and its text says so. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no prefix, since the `##` header *is* the
  bare title. The as-built ladder is the first content under it (see
  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose
  (see [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim. Pick the commit title first and
reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

**Cycle bookend titles**: the opening commit's title is the close-out title plus " opening",
same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` / `feat: dynamic warmup`), so one
`git log --grep "<close-out title>"` returns exactly the pair that brackets the cycle. The
type repeats the close-out's even though an opening is mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes
make the pair scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.

### Steps are named, not numbered

A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung, a chores as-built rung, a `## Done`
entry, or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a rung's place in the list already *is* its place in
the ladder, so a number beside it would restate the position and then have to be maintained.

- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable in the two places a
  title is resolved: within its own cycle, so a ladder rung names one step, and within its chores
  file, since a `##` header is also an anchor and a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first
  one. Across the repo's history a title may repeat.
- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and
  nothing else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder
  come along. See
  [Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
- **`## Todo` ranks are the exception that stays numbered**, because a priority list has an order
  worth reading off (see [Todo format](notes.md#todo-format)). Those numbers are positional too,
  and are equally never used as references.

### Versions live in the version-of-record only

No version appears in durable prose: not in an in-flight ladder rung, a chores header, a commit
title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only written home (see
[versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from that file at that
commit.

**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.

**Two surfaces record a version rather than name a step.** Both record a *commit*, never a step,
which is what keeps them outside the rule rather than exceptions to it:

- **A chores as-built rung** records a version alongside that commit's SHA once the commit is on
  a permanent branch. The pair decodes an old `-V` banner or a pasted report. It obeys the SHA's
  timing exactly, so a rung on an unlanded branch carries neither (see
  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **A `## Done` entry**, in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`, carries the close-out's version ahead of
  its title (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Here the version is the search
  key: the question a reader arrives with is "what shipped in 0.42.0", and with no version
  written anywhere in the Done list that question has no answer.

The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
because a commit cannot record its own SHA; a Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
([Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)), and a renumber of
published versions rewrites it in the same sweep as the rungs.

**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
opening"). Writing *about* versioning is unaffected: a version named as a specimen, whether in the
scheme's own notation, a decoder table, or a narrative about a renumber, is a use of the word
rather than an identifier for a step, the same distinction
[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws between naming a character and using
one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.

## Pinned files name no project

A pinned agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names a member project, a member's
history, or a member's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every member
shares and stay. What is barred is a member repo appearing in universal text.

**Why:** pinned text is copied to every member, so a project narration reads as the reader's own
history ("This project adopted the convention on <date>" arrives in repos that adopted it on a
different date or never). And the citation goes stale the moment the named project retires its
records, while the rule outlives it.

**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file; leave the evidence trail
in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
specimen in
the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
reference, per the same distinction
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
draws.

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
worth keeping visible in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
synopsis.

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed
7	change is edited here and converges at the template
8	([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
12	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
13	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
14	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning). Substitute your medium's
15	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
16	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
17	
18	## Cycles
19	
20	A cycle has three phases:
21	
22	- **[Preparation](#preparation)**: the cycle's first commit,
23	  when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits it and
24	  starts at its first Work step). Sets up the cycle:
25	  - Bump the version-of-record (where it lives and the
26	    suffix scheme are project-specific, per
27	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
28	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked, #1)
29	    into `## In Progress` as the cycle's
30	    [six provisional items](#preparation): title, problem
31	    statement, solution statement, acceptance check, ladder,
32	    deliberation.
33	  - Create the cycle's topic bookmark.
34	  - Nothing is opened in the chores file. The block is the
35	    cycle's only home until close-out moves it.
36	- **[Work-N](#work-n)**: the commits that implement the
37	  change. As many as the change needs. Each runs through the
38	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
39	- **[Close-out](#close-out)**: the cycle's last commit.
40	  Bookkeeping only:
41	  - Run the acceptance check and record what it showed.
42	  - Finalize the six items, then move the block into
43	    `notes/chores/`, which creates the
44	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
45	  - Write the `## Done` entry and clear `## In Progress`.
46	  - Land the cycle's bookmark.
47	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
48	    changed.
49	
50	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
51	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out. The
52	result must always be published at close-out. See
53	[Pushing](#pushing).
54	
55	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
56	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides into its own
57	Preparation / Work / Close-out. The same three-phase shape
58	applies recursively at every depth, and a sub-ladder's rungs
59	are titles like any other. See
60	[Step naming](#step-naming) for how a step is identified and
61	[Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the local-ladder
62	mechanics.
63	
64	## Chores sections
65	
66	A **chores section** is a `##` section in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work.
67	In general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch should have a rung in some
68	section's as-built ladder in a chores file.
69	
70	**A cycle's record has one home at a time.** While the cycle runs it lives entirely in
71	`TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the [six provisional items](#preparation) written at Preparation
72	and revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block **moves** into the chores file, becoming
73	that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in two places, so there is nothing to keep in
74	sync and nothing to write twice.
75	
76	The move is mechanical, four transforms and no rewriting:
77	
78	- **Heading levels shift so the title becomes the section's `##`** and the items shift with it,
79	  staying one level under the title. Anchors survive untouched, because GitHub slugs derive from
80	  the heading's *text*, not its level. The depth shift is one level for a plain cycle, and
81	  whatever the title's depth demands under a program heading.
82	- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]` namespace (see
83	  [Reference numbering](notes.md#reference-numbering)).
84	- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block moves from the root into
85	  `notes/chores/`.
86	- **The block's own forward-looking notes are rewritten**, since they described a future that
87	  has now happened.
88	
89	Two of those fail *silently*: a mis-renumbered ref and an un-rebased link render as plain text
90	or a 404 rather than erroring. Check both by hand until a `validate-repo` exists.
91	
92	A single-commit cycle's ladder is one rung, its close-out. Rung placeholders are backfilled once
93	the commit is permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
94	
95	The move also appends the section's title-only `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
96	`## Table of Contents`.
97	
98	Adopted after a full-cycle trial: the dual maintenance disappeared, and the narrative did not
99	thin out from being written in `TODO.md`, which was the watched-for risk.
100	
101	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync, design subsection pattern, ladder and
102	reference formatting, the Table of Contents) live in
103	[Chores conventions](notes.md#chores-conventions).
104	
105	### Commits backfill
106	
107	An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA and records the version that commit carried,
108	and neither is stable until the commit lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
109	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten). A rebase or squash rewrites the SHA and may
110	renumber the version on the way. So:
111	
112	- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version**.
113	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where both are final. A commit
114	  can't record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push
115	  later: **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On
116	  a topic branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so nothing is ever written
117	  that a later rebase could invalidate.
118	- A deliberate rewrite of already-recorded commits (a coordinated re-describe, a retroactive
119	  reshape) invalidates their recorded SHAs. Re-record them once the rewrite is published, on
120	  the same one-push-later timing.
121	
122	Backfill replaces the placeholder with a real file-local `[N]` slot, defined as the commit URL +
123	40-hex SHA in the file's `# References` (format in
124	[Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)), and writes the version ahead of
125	the title. A section's `##` title matches its close-out commit title, and each rung's text its
126	own commit title, so a rare deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
127	`git log --grep "<title>"`. Sections that predate the ladder form keep their grandfathered
128	`Commits:` lines. Backfill those where they exist.
129	
130	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A **per-close-out** model (recording a
131	cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: what a rung records must be
132	permanent.
133	
134	## Preparation
135	
136	The cycle's first commit, when the cycle needs setup (a
137	lightweight cycle omits it, per
138	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)):
139	
140	- **Create the cycle's topic bookmark** (commands in
141	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
142	- **Bump the version-of-record.** Where it lives, the suffix
143	  scheme, and any derived files (a lockfile, a sourced
144	  manifest version) are project-specific. See
145	  [versioning.md](versioning.md).
146	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
147	  `## In Progress`, and write the cycle's **six provisional
148	  items** there. All six are required, all six are revised
149	  as steps land, and all six move to chores at close-out.
150	  The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
151	  own, and the other five are headings one level below the
152	  title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items; under a
153	  program heading, each one deeper):
154	  - the **title**, which becomes the chores section header.

1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## The cycle at a glance
13	
14	Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
15	phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
16	individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional); a
17	**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
18	that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties, mandatory validation included. The
19	ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
20	version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
21	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
22	work, and before any push, cycle or not.
23	
24	## Cycles run on a bookmark
25	
26	A cycle runs on its own topic bookmark, created at the opening and named for the cycle. `main`
27	advances only by landing one. Nothing pushes straight to `main`.
28	
29	- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
30	  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
31	  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
32	  that makes the cycle permanent.
33	- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
34	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
35	  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
36	- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
37	  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
38	- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
39	  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
40	  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).
41	
42	**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
43	published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.
44	
45	## Opening checklist
46	
47	At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:
48	
49	1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
50	2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
51	   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
52	   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
53	   title, `####` items; under a program heading, each one deeper):
54	   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
55	   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
56	   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
57	   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
58	   - **ladder**: one rung per step, bare title plus `(current)` / `(done)`
59	   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
60	     deliberate)
61	3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
62	   version-of-record.
63	
64	Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
65	moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
66	
67	**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
68	of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
69	against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
70	sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
71	the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
72	done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
73	same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.
74	
75	## Committing vs pushing
76	
77	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
78	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
79	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
80	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
81	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
82	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
83	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
84	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
85	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
86	
87	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
88	
89	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
90	So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
91	the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.
92	
93	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
94	  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
95	  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
96	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
97	- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
98	  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
99	  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
100	
101	The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
102	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
103	[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
104
