1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## The cycle at a glance
13	
14	Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
15	phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
16	individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional); a
17	**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
18	that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties, mandatory validation included. The
19	ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
20	version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
21	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
22	work, and before any push, cycle or not.
23	
24	## Cycles run on a bookmark
25	
26	A cycle runs on its own topic bookmark, created at the opening and named for the cycle. `main`
27	advances only by landing one. Nothing pushes straight to `main`.
28	
29	- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
30	  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
31	  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
32	  that makes the cycle permanent.
33	- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
34	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
35	  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
36	- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
37	  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
38	- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
39	  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
40	  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).
41	
42	**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
43	published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.
44	
45	## Opening checklist
46	
47	At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:
48	
49	1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
50	2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
51	   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
52	   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
53	   title, `####` items; under a program heading, each one deeper):
54	   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
55	   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
56	   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
57	   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
58	   - **ladder**: one rung per step, bare title plus `(current)` / `(done)`
59	   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
60	     deliberate)
61	3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
62	   version-of-record.
63	
64	Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
65	moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
66	
67	**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
68	of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
69	against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
70	sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
71	the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
72	done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
73	same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.
74	
75	## Committing vs pushing
76	
77	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
78	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
79	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
80	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
81	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
82	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
83	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
84	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
85	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
86	
87	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
88	
89	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
90	So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
91	the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.
92	
93	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
94	  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
95	  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
96	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
97	- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
98	  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
99	  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
100	
101	The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
102	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
103	[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
104	
105	## Per-commit checklist
106	
107	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
108	[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
109	
110	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
111	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
112	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
113	4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
114	   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
115	   commit.
116	5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
117	   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
118	6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
119	   a description as we iterate until the user reviews says "continue|go|.." indicating cycle is likely
120	   complete.
121	7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a problem
122	   statement and a solution statement, both broad, sized per prose.md's
123	   [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
124	   mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo, and the session hold that). See

- the bot-communication guidance adds that the Work review message
  holds no title or body

318	# The entry that resolves to this config's own directory names the

Thoughts, no changes made.

**The attraction is real.** A prototype `.vc-config.toml` in the repo makes the generated artifact WYSIWYG — you review the actual file users will get, not Rust string-building. And url/reference edits become TOML edits, no recompile, which the family could even do from the template side.

**But it inverts the drift protection this cycle exists to fix.** The fossil `[push]` block rotted precisely because file content wasn't tied to the binary. The current design's one virtue is that `init.rs` renders from `config_schema::schema()` "so this list cannot drift from the schema." A prototype file as generator *input* recreates the two-sources-of-truth problem: the schema (keys, types, defaults, validation) must stay in code because `config.rs` parses and `--validate` checks against it, so a prototype carrying key blocks + urls can silently disagree with the code — the exact disease, one layer up. There's also a practical snag: the installed binary runs far from this repo, so `vc-x1 config` couldn't print the urls unless the prototype is embedded at build time — at which point it's code again, just less checkable.

**A middle path gets you both properties:**

- **Urls live in the schema**: `config_schema.rs` gains a `reference` field per key, rendered as a `#   reference: <url>` line everywhere the schema is emitted (`config` print, generated files, `--refresh`). One source of truth; a test can even check that repo-relative targets exist.
- **The prototype becomes a golden file, not an input**: commit the rendered `.vc-config.toml` prototype and have a snapshot test assert `render_vc_config()` matches it. You get the reviewable in-repo file, and drift becomes a *failing test* instead of silent rot — the data flows code -> file, never file -> code.
- **Per-project prototypes already have a mechanism**: `init --config <file>` copies a user-supplied config verbatim, so a family-customized prototype can live in the template payload and ride `--use-template`, no new machinery.

One thing to settle regardless of where the data lives: what the urls point at. Repo-relative paths (`notes/README.md#...`) only resolve inside this repo; a generated config in a user's project probably wants hosted urls (github blob links), which are editable but rot on restructures.

Also, clarifying: by "this repo" did you mean vc-x1 itself or the template repository? If the template, the golden-file + `--use-template` combination above is basically your idea with the arrow flipped.

The plain version: keep the machine-readable truth in the code, but also commit the generated file so humans can see it, and add a test that screams if the two ever disagree. Your idea's benefits survive; its drift risk doesn't.

Ah — so the arrow points the other way: the file is the master, and the binary's generation code derives from it (embedded at build time, presumably). Thoughts on that version:

**It genuinely kills drift only if the binary's *behavior* also derives from the file.** The keys, defaults, and doc text live twice today: in `config_schema.rs` (the table `config` prints and `--validate` checks) and in behavioral constants like `COL_WIDTH: usize = 68` in `bot_session.rs`. If the prototype only feeds the *generator*, then someone changes `COL_WIDTH` to 72 in code and the shipped binary now generates a config that documents 68 while behaving 72 — drift again, just relocated. The strong form of your idea is: build.rs parses the prototype, generates the Rust schema table from it, and the commands read their defaults *from that table* — then the file is the single truth and the code physically cannot disagree. That's real architecture, and arguably better than today's: one defaults table, docs and behavior from one source.

**Two frictions with using the live `.vc-config.toml` itself as that master:**

- Its documentation is *comments*. Build-time parsing of prose-shaped comment blocks (`#   default: 10`, `#   reference: ...`) is fragile in a way real TOML values aren't. A spec wants to be data.
- It's a live config with repo-specific `[repos]` values, so the generator must treat that block specially per role (work/bot/single) — the file can't be used verbatim, and editing your working config becomes editing the product spec, which will surprise someone eventually.

**The robust variant**: a dedicated `config-schema.toml` in the repo — real TOML tables per key: path, doc, used-by, default, url — embedded via build.rs into the generated Rust table. The `.vc-config.toml` files everywhere (this repo's included) are then *rendered* from it, so they're golden files a snapshot test keeps honest. You still get everything you're after: docs and urls editable as TOML without touching Rust, the repo showing exactly what users receive, and no drift by construction. What changes from your phrasing is only which file is the prototype: a spec file, with the live config as its first rendered output.

content.text:
I like it, with three design adjustments that keep the idea intact but avoid known potholes.

**The shape of the file.** Make `vc-config.toml` mirror the config's own structure, one level richer — each settable key becomes a table whose entries are its metadata:

```toml
[bot-session.col-width]
doc = "Default --col-width: first-column width in the field-inventory views"
used-by = "bot-session --col-width"
default = 68
reference = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/main/notes/README.md#bot-session"
```

That's real parseable TOML (no comment-parsing), and it genuinely *is* the prototype of a vc-config: same skeleton (`section.leaf`), so a reader sees the correspondence at a glance. The `repos.*` keys ride along with `required = true` and no default, keeping the existing special-casing honest.

**Generate into OUT_DIR, not into `src/`.** build.rs overwriting a tracked `src/config_schema.rs` is the classic anti-pattern: dirty trees on every build and rebuild loops. Instead build.rs emits the schema table into `$OUT_DIR`, and `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to `include!(...)` plus the hand-written helpers (`render_key_block`, `section_and_leaf`). Plus `cargo::rerun-if-changed=vc-config.toml`, and malformed or incomplete key tables become *build errors* — schema validation moves to compile time, which is a nice upgrade.

**Close the loop on behavioral defaults, or the drift survives.** This is the part that makes it worth doing: build.rs should also emit the defaults as constants (`BOT_SESSION_COL_WIDTH_DEFAULT: usize = 68`) and `bot_session.rs` et al. consume *those*, retiring the hand-kept `COL_WIDTH` / `RESULT_LINE_CAP`. Otherwise the file documents 68 while the code decides independently, and we've rebuilt today's drift with extra steps. (The clap help strings that hand-say "[default: 68...]" can take expressions, so they can be fed from the same constants.)

Two flags, both mild: `vc-config.toml` next to `.vc-config.toml` will make someone edit the wrong one eventually — the header comment should say loudly "this is the schema prototype, your config is `.vc-config.toml`"; and build.rs gains a `toml` build-dependency plus codegen code, complexity that's real but contained.

**Scope.** This is cycle-sized and it supersedes the current cycle's remaining approach: `chore: regenerate stale config files` would regenerate from the new pipeline, and `config --refresh` would render from the generated schema. The two landed rungs (the review-stop docs) stand on their own regardless. So the natural move is to re-scope this cycle: revert my uncommitted config regeneration, rewrite the ladder around the prototype (roughly: `feat: vc-config.toml prototype + build.rs codegen`, then regenerate, then `--refresh`, then `.agent-session`), and record the pivot in the deliberation. The alternative — land the modest version first, prototype cycle after — means regenerating the configs twice and writing `--refresh` against a schema module about to be replaced, which is work we'd knowingly throw away.

The plain version: your file-drives-the-code idea is sound if the file is structured data, the generated code goes in the build's scratch area, and the program's own defaults come from the generated code too — then nothing can disagree with the file. It's big enough to become this cycle's new plan rather than a side fix.

### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Problem

Both repos' `.vc-config.toml` carry a fossil `[push]` comment block from an older binary's
schema, the retired `.vc-x1` state dirs linger (empty dirs on disk, a `/.vc-x1` line in the
work `.gitignore`), generated config comments have no refresh tooling so they rot silently, and
the bot dir's `.claude` name is agent-specific where this workspace wants the neutral
`.agent-session`.

#### Solution

Regenerate both config files from the current binary's schema, retire the state-dir leftovers,
add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving active
keys and `[repos]`, and repoint `repos.bot` at `.agent-session`. The directory rename itself is
wink's move between sessions (a live session writes through the symlink), with the following
session committing the record.

#### Acceptance check

1. `vc-x1 config --validate` is clean on both sides, and neither file mentions `[push]`,
   `state-dir`, or `state-file`.
2. `config --refresh` on a fixture with stale comment blocks and active keys preserves the
   active keys and `[repos]` while replacing the stale blocks (a test demonstrates it).
3. After the rename: `repos.bot = ".agent-session"`, a cycle rung pushes from a session end to
   end, and new commits still stamp `/.claude/`-labeled ochid trailers.
4. No `.vc-x1` dir in either repo and no `/.vc-x1` line in `.gitignore`, which ignores the bot
   dir under its new name.

#### Ladder

- docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd opening (done)
- docs: separate work review stop (done)
- chore: regenerate stale config files (done)
- feat: add config --refresh
- chore: point config at .agent-session
  - wink's between-session move sits just before this rung: after the previous rung lands
    and the bot tail is flushed, /exit, then `mv .claude .agent-session`, edit the work-side
    config's `repos.bot` and the work `.gitignore` entry to `.agent-session`, run
    `vc-x1 symlink`, and start the session that commits this rung
  - the `.gitignore` edit belongs in the move, not the commit: un-ignored, the renamed bot
    dir would be swept into the work repo's next snapshot
- docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Deliberation

- the `.agent-session` rename was leaning toward its own cycle; it folds in here because it
  needs an inter-session quiesce, which a multi-step cycle's `/exit` between rungs naturally
  provides
- the ochid prefix is a canonical side label decoupled from the bot dir's path (test-pinned: a
  custom bot dir still stamps `/.claude/`), so history and future trailers stay coherent across
  the rename
- pinned files name `.claude` as the bot repo's path; the rename step updates that text to
  path-neutral wording as a family proposal, this member's diff carrying it until convergence
- 0.79.0 is spoken for by the trapezoid branch's anticipated close-out, so this cycle is a
  patch at 0.78.8
- the close-out title dropped ".toml" from wink's phrasing so the opening bookend stays inside
  the title cap
- the single-name guard refuses a suffixed version under the stable name, so the opening
  renames the package to `vc-x1-dev` (versioning.md's Dev artifact name) and the close-out's
  bump to the bare version renames it back
- Done sweep at this opening: nothing migrated, the 0.78.2+ entries staying as nearby context
  after the 0.78.6 sweep
- the "docs: separate work review stop" rung was inserted at this opening's own review, where
  the bot collapsed the work review and the description review into one message. The rule
  already stands in the checklist and protocol; the rung sharpens both so no description
  appears before the work review settles. An agent-file change is its own commit, which is why
  it is a rung rather than a rider on the opening

message.content: Note the bot-session.col-width will be <=100, I assume 100 will work for .toml tools like jq?

content.text:
Two different widths are in play here, so let me separate them and then answer the compatibility question.

**`bot-session.col-width` is a display width, not a file property.** It's the width of the *first column* in `bot-session`'s `--fields` / `--unknown` / `--per-line` views — the column holding JSONL key paths like `message.content.text`, with the type/count info starting after it. It never touches any file on disk; it only shapes vc-x1's own terminal output. 68 was measured to fit ~99% of observed key paths. Setting it to 100 works mechanically — the views just get wider — but it pushes the type column past the edge of a standard 80-col terminal and pads most rows with blanks, so as a *default* 68 is probably still the better fit, with `--col-width` (or the config key) there for wider terminals.

**Tools don't care about either width.** TOML parsers (taplo, `toml` crates) and jq (which would be reading the session JSONL, not the TOML) have no line-length limits at all — 100, 200, or one giant line are all equally parseable. Line width matters only to human readers, which is why our <=100 rule lives in prose.md rather than in any tool's constraints.

**Where 100 does become relevant to the prototype**: the generated comment blocks currently wrap around ~72 (you can see it in the `config` output). When the renderer is rebuilt in the prototype rung, its wrap width can adopt the consolidated <=100 prose rule — wider, fewer continuation lines, and nothing downstream objects.

If you meant something else by "col-width will be <=100" — say, recording a max-value *constraint* on the key in the prototype (the schema tables could carry `min`/`max` and validate them) — that's easy to add to the design; tell me and I'll fold it into the block.

The plain version: col-width only shapes how one command's tables look on your screen; no file or tool ever sees it. Parsers ignore line lengths entirely, so wrapping the generated comments at 100 is safe. Which of the two widths did you want changed?

content.text:
Not dumb — that's the key's discoverability failing, not you; a third data point for the reference-link work.

On OSC 8: right mechanism, wrong storage location. Splitting it:

**Embedding OSC 8 in the files themselves would work for `cat` — and break everything else.** OSC 8 links are literal escape sequences (`ESC ] 8 ; ; url ESC \ text ...`), so the file would carry raw ESC control bytes. TOML forbids control characters other than tab in comments, so the file becomes spec-invalid — strict parsers can reject it outright. And every non-terminal consumer degrades: editors show the escape bytes as noise in the buffer, diffs and greps get contaminated, `less` without `-R` prints `^[]8;;` litter. All that to improve one command, `cat`.

**Plain URLs already get you most of it.** A `#   reference: https://...` line is auto-linkified nearly everywhere today: Zed and VS Code make bare URLs in file buffers ctrl-clickable, and most modern terminals (kitty, WezTerm, iTerm2, foot, GNOME Terminal) detect URLs in output and make them clickable without OSC 8. So the prototype's plain-URL reference lines are probably clickable for you on day one, at zero cost.

**Where OSC 8 genuinely fits: vc-x1's own output.** `vc-x1 config` prints the schema — *it* can emit OSC 8 when stdout is a TTY, e.g. making each key name itself a link to its reference url, with the sequences suppressed when piped (the `ls --hyperlink=auto` convention). Output is ephemeral and terminal-bound, so escapes are appropriate there in a way they aren't in a stored file. Zed's integrated terminal is built on the same terminal core as Alacritty, which grew OSC 8 support, so there's a fair chance it renders them; easy to probe with a one-liner:

```
printf '\e]8;;https://example.com\e\\click me\e]8;;\e\\\n'
```

The plain version: put ordinary URLs in the files — editors and most terminals already make those clickable. Save the fancy escape-code links for what `vc-x1 config` prints to the screen, where they belong and can be turned off when piping. Putting escape codes inside the TOML file would make the file technically invalid and ugly everywhere except `cat`.

Scope-wise, TTY hyperlinks in `config` output is a tidy little feature that builds on the prototype's reference field — I'd capture it as a `notes/todo-backlog.md` entry rather than grow this cycle further. Want me to add it?

Hmm, you say "- behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
    code cannot disagree with the file". That implies to me that vc-config.toml (prototype) is going to be edited.
But I'm thinking we are going to commit it so it can be use to iterate .vc-config.toml. The solution is part of the vc-x1 commit "Acceptance check" is running the "generation" and verify nothing changes. Thoughts only.

content.text:
Yes to all of it — and I think we're describing the same design from two ends; let me line the pieces up.

**`vc-config.toml` is committed source, full stop.** It's edited the way `main.rs` is edited: in commits, reviewed like code, because it *is* code now — the master the binary is compiled from. The sentence you quoted describes what that mastery buys at build time: build.rs re-derives the schema table and constants from the file on every compile, so the *binary* can't disagree with the *file at that commit*. It's not about anyone editing the file at runtime; agreement is by construction, not by policing.

**Two derivations hang off it, and they drift differently:**

- **file -> binary** (build.rs, OUT_DIR): can't drift — every build re-derives, and `rerun-if-changed` makes edits take effect immediately.
- **file -> committed `.vc-config.toml`s** (the rendered, commented user-facing configs): *can* drift, because those are checked-in artifacts a human must remember to regenerate after editing the prototype.

**Your acceptance-check idea closes exactly that second gap, and I'd adopt it verbatim**: run the generation and verify nothing changes. The natural vehicle is the `--refresh` rung — a `config --refresh --check` mode (the `cargo fmt --check` convention) that renders what the files *should* say, compares, and exits nonzero on any difference without writing. That gives three things at once: the acceptance check is a single runnable command, the close-out validation can include it permanently, and `--refresh` gets its own test surface for free. The `[repos]` blocks stay exempt by the same preserve-active-keys rule refresh already promises.

So the flow end to end: edit `vc-config.toml` in a commit -> the next build makes the binary agree automatically -> `config --refresh` makes the `.vc-config.toml`s agree -> `--refresh --check` proves they agree, and screams when someone edited the prototype and skipped the refresh.

The plain version: the prototype is a normal committed file and the single place truth lives. The compiler keeps the program in sync with it automatically; the check command keeps the generated config files in sync by complaining loudly when they're stale. Your "run generation, verify nothing changes" is that check.

When you're happy with the shape, say the word and I'll fold `--refresh --check` into the solution bullets and acceptance check.

Just so `vc-x1 config --refresh --check` is our "Acceptance check", but the user should be able to use it too, although it won't modify the source unless the clone/fork the source. But it still seems useful?

content.text:
Still useful — arguably *more* useful for them than for us, and it's the same command doing the same thing; only the situation differs.

The key point: `--check` doesn't need the prototype file at runtime. The schema it compares against is baked into whatever binary is installed (build.rs derived it from the prototype at compile time). So in any project, `vc-x1 config --refresh --check` answers "are this repo's config comment blocks current for the binary I'm running?" — no vc-x1 source required.

That gives each audience a different story with one flag:

- **Us**: the acceptance check — committed configs match what the committed prototype renders, run at close-out and in validation.
- **A user after upgrading vc-x1**: their config's comment block was written by the *old* binary; `--check` says whether it's gone stale, `--refresh` brings it current while keeping their active keys. That's precisely the fossil-`[push]`-block story, which sat unnoticed in *this* repo for multiple versions — the tool would have caught it the day the schema changed.
- **The family**: exit-code semantics make it sweepable — run `--check` across member repos to find stale configs mechanically.

And you're right about the boundary: a user's `--refresh` only ever rewrites *their own config file's* comments. If what they disagree with is the schema itself — a default, a doc line — that's upstream, via fork/PR against the prototype. Nice property: the prototype being a TOML file rather than Rust makes that PR approachable for non-Rust users.

The plain version: the check works anywhere because the binary carries its own schema; users get a "has my config's documentation gone stale since I upgraded?" probe, and we get our acceptance check, from the same flag.

The block's wording already covers this (the solution bullet describes `--refresh` as a general CLI feature; item 4 is just our use of it), so I'd leave the text as is unless you want the upgrade story called out explicitly.

#   doc        one-line description (rendered, keep it tight)

- **Drift guards**: new tests assert the clap help text's `[default: N; ...]` notes match the generated defaults, that `parse_item_list(items-default) == ItemSet::BUILTIN`, and that every key has an https reference; the old `defaults_match_source_consts` test became a codegen self-check.

content.text:
Agreed on the goal — the review summary shouldn't evaporate into the session transcript; it should ride the block into chores. But I'd put it in the **Ladder**, not the Deliberation, and here's the reasoning.

**Deliberation is for decisions, not descriptions.** Its definition is "how the five above were decided, alternatives weighed, costs accepted." A per-rung "what it built" entry is descriptive — it answers *what happened*, not *what was chosen and why*. Filling Deliberation with build summaries would bury the actual decisions (and this cycle's Deliberation is already long from the pivot). Notably, Deliberation *already* accretes per-rung entries when a rung produces a real decision — the review-stop rung's insertion, the pivot, `--check`'s origin all got bullets. That's event-driven, and I'd keep it that way: a mechanical rung ("chore: regenerate...") may legitimately contribute nothing, and forcing a slot per rung invites filler.

**The Ladder already supports per-rung detail, positionally.** prose.md's shape allows bulleted detail under a rung (the `.agent-session` rung carries sub-bullets today). Sub-bullets under the rung need no name-matching to a parallel list, they move to chores inside the block, and at close-out they become exactly the as-built ladder detail the chores conventions want — conceptual bullets "a notch above file-list granularity," which chores explicitly prefers over edit lists (the diff is the mechanical record; my review summary would be trimmed to its conceptual half).

**Timing**: write them at the rung's completion, while fresh — consistent with "all six revised as steps land," and it beats reconstructing narrative at close-out from memory. Concretely it would slot into per-commit flow step 3: flip `(current)` to `(done)` *and* write the rung's conceptual sub-bullets.

**One caution**: the commit body already carries each rung's problem + solution. The sub-bullets should hold the *delta* — design points and consequences (line-based parser to keep build.rs dependency-free, codegen to OUT_DIR not `src/`, wrap-width deferred to the regenerate rung) — not restate the body.

Since ladder sub-bullets are already legal, we can practice this immediately with no rule change; if it earns its keep, the step-3 amendment to the pinned checklist/protocol is a family proposal, its own commit, like the review-stop rung was.

The plain version: keep "what we decided" in Deliberation and put "what each step built" as indented notes right under that step in the ladder, written when the step finishes. The whole block moves to the chores file at close-out, so nothing is lost — and the two kinds of information stay findable instead of mixed.

Want me to backfill sub-bullets for the three landed rungs and adopt the practice for the rest of this cycle?

content.text:
That solves the wordiness cleanly, and it rhymes with machinery we already have — the chores file's Table of Contents is exactly this pattern (title-only entries pointing at title-named sections). Extending it into the cycle block:

**Shape**: the Ladder stays bare rungs + markers, a ToC. A rung that has something worth recording gets a section headed by its *exact title*, sitting after Deliberation (so the six canonical items stay contiguous, and the sections trail like the design subsections chores already grows). The title-identity rule then holds in four places instead of three — ladder rung, rung section heading, commit title, chores header — one `grep "<title>"` finds them all, and the heading is a real anchor other records can link to.

**What this buys over my sub-bullets idea**: scannability (the ladder answers "where are we" at a glance again), addressability (Deliberation, bugs.md, the backlog can point at `#feat-vc-configtoml-prototype--buildrs-codegen` instead of describing it), and optionality without raggedness — a mechanical rung simply has no section, which reads fine, whereas a ladder where some rungs have sub-bullet beards and some don't reads lumpy.

**Details to pin down:**

- **No placeholder sections.** A section exists only when a rung has conceptual content. The ToC doesn't promise one per rung.
- **Written at rung completion**, same timing argument as before — while fresh, revised like everything else in the block.
- **Content is the delta**, not the commit body restated: design points, consequences, deferrals.
- **Heading depth**: in a plain cycle the sections sit at the items' level (`####`); everything shifts one deeper at the close-out move, as the four transforms already do. Under a program heading a sub-cycle could brush markdown's `######` floor — rare, worth a note when we pin it.
- **The `.agent-session` rung's sub-bullets** would migrate to its section for uniformity — though as forward-looking *plan* notes they're arguably ladder-legal either way; migrating is tidier.

**Adoption path**: nothing pinned forbids this today (it's the design-subsection pattern with disciplined naming), so we can practice it in this cycle's block immediately. If it earns its keep by close-out, pinning it — cycle-protocol's Preparation/Chores sections, prose.md's shape, the checklists — is a family proposal, its own docs rung, same route the review-stop rung took.

The plain version: the ladder becomes a clean table of contents; each step that deserves notes gets its own little chapter named exactly after the step, so searching the step's name finds the plan line, the notes, and the commit together. Steps with nothing to say just don't get a chapter.

Want me to apply it now — add the prototype rung's section, migrate the `.agent-session` bullets, and we see how it reads?

### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Problem

Both repos' `.vc-config.toml` carry a fossil `[push]` comment block from an older binary's
schema, the retired `.vc-x1` state dirs linger (empty dirs on disk, a `/.vc-x1` line in the
work `.gitignore`), generated config comments have no refresh tooling so they rot silently, and
the bot dir's `.claude` name is agent-specific where this workspace wants the neutral
`.agent-session`.

#### Solution

Make a repo-root `vc-config.toml` prototype the schema's single source, then rebuild the
config surface from it:

- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
  reference url
- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
    code cannot disagree with the file
- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
- retire the state-dir leftovers
- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving
  active keys and `[repos]`
  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
- repoint `repos.bot` at `.agent-session`
  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record

#### Acceptance check

1. build.rs generates the schema table and default constants from `vc-config.toml`
   (rerun-if-changed wired), the hand-kept `COL_WIDTH` / `RESULT_LINE_CAP` constants are gone
   from `src/`, and generated configs carry each key's `reference:` line.
2. `vc-x1 config --validate` is clean on both sides, and neither file mentions `[push]`,
   `state-dir`, or `state-file`.
3. `config --refresh` on a fixture with stale comment blocks and active keys preserves the
   active keys and `[repos]` while replacing the stale blocks (a test demonstrates it).
4. `config --refresh --check` exits clean on both sides, proving the committed config files
   match what the prototype renders.
5. After the rename: `repos.bot = ".agent-session"`, a cycle rung pushes from a session end to
   end, and new commits still stamp `/.claude/`-labeled ochid trailers.
6. No `.vc-x1` dir in either repo and no `/.vc-x1` line in `.gitignore`, which ignores the bot
   dir under its new name.

#### Ladder

- docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd opening (done)
- docs: separate work review stop (done)
- feat: vc-config.toml prototype + build.rs codegen (done)
- chore: regenerate stale config files
- feat: add config --refresh
- chore: point config at .agent-session
- docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Deliberation

- the `.agent-session` rename was leaning toward its own cycle; it folds in here because it
  needs an inter-session quiesce, which a multi-step cycle's `/exit` between rungs naturally
  provides
- the ochid prefix is a canonical side label decoupled from the bot dir's path (test-pinned: a
  custom bot dir still stamps `/.claude/`), so history and future trailers stay coherent across
  the rename
- pinned files name `.claude` as the bot repo's path; the rename step updates that text to
  path-neutral wording as a family proposal, this member's diff carrying it until convergence
- 0.79.0 is spoken for by the trapezoid branch's anticipated close-out, so this cycle is a
  patch at 0.78.8
- the close-out title dropped ".toml" from wink's phrasing so the opening bookend stays inside
  the title cap
- the single-name guard refuses a suffixed version under the stable name, so the opening
  renames the package to `vc-x1-dev` (versioning.md's Dev artifact name) and the close-out's
  bump to the bare version renames it back
- Done sweep at this opening: nothing migrated, the 0.78.2+ entries staying as nearby context

### config

Print the settable config keys for a target config file as an annotated, commented schema: for each
key its description, the command/context it's `used by`, its default (or a value marked `# example`
when there is no default), and a commented assignment line ready to paste in. The schema is
generated from one in-code registry, so it can't drift from what the code actually reads.

- `[TARGET]`: `work`, `bot`, `work,bot` (default), or an explicit config-file path. The keywords
  resolve against the surrounding workspace's `.vc-config.toml` files and filter to that side's
  keys; a path carries no side information, so it gets the whole schema. The user config
  (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`) has no keyword and is reached only by passing its path.
- `--validate`: instead of printing, load the target's actual config file(s) and flag any key the
  schema doesn't recognize (a typo, a key in the wrong section, or an unknown key), plus, for
  keyword targets, the legacy-schema rejection and the resolved-agreement invariant of a dual
  workspace's `[repos]` registries. Exits non-zero if any problem is found. This is an opt-in strict
  check; a normal config load silently ignores unknown keys, for forward-compatibility.

A short sample of the printed schema (workspace home):

```
[bot-session]
# bot-session.col-width: Default --col-width: first-column width in the
#   field-inventory views
#   used by: bot-session --col-width
#   default: 68
# col-width = 68

[repos]
# repos.work: The work repo's path, relative to this config file's
#   directory ("." in the work repo, ".." in the bot repo); the entry
#   resolving to the config's own directory names the side
#   used by: find_workspace_root, side detection (structural; written by init)
#   default: (required; role-specific, see init)
work = "."   # example
```

A key with no default (`default.account`, in the user home) instead renders a commented example
value:

# default.account: Account profile (an [account.<name>] section) to use
#   when --account is absent
#   used by: --account (init and account-aware commands)
#   default: (none)
# account = "work"   # example

### vc-config.toml (the schema prototype)

`vc-config.toml` at the repo root (no leading dot) is the single source of truth for the settable-key
schema above. It is not a config file: each settable key is a TOML table of that key's metadata, and
build.rs parses the file and generates the schema table plus the built-in default constants the
binary compiles against. One file drives every surface:

- the `config` subcommand's printed schema (above)
- the commented blocks `init` writes into a new workspace's `.vc-config.toml`
- the built-in defaults themselves (e.g. `bot-session --col-width`'s 68), consumed from the
  generated constants, so behavior cannot disagree with documentation
- each key's `reference:` url, so a reader of any generated config can find that key's docs

Editing the prototype is a source change like any other: edit, `cargo build`, and the change is live
(build.rs re-runs whenever the file changes). A malformed prototype, an unknown metadata entry, a
missing `doc` or `reference`, a non-integer `usize` default, or a duplicate key path fails the build
with a message naming the offending table. A key's table looks like:

used-by = "bot-session --col-width"
reference = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/main/README.md#bot-session"

content.text:
Two separate questions in there — one gets a no, the other a yes-and-it-improves-the-design.

**Fully relative references break exactly where they're needed.** The reference line renders in three places: this repo (relative would work), `vc-x1 config` output on any machine, and generated `.vc-config.toml` files in *users'* repos. In those last two, `README.md#bot-session` resolves against the user's own directory, where no such docs exist. The https url is the only address that's valid from everywhere, which is why I went hosted.

**But `vc-config.md` is better than what I built, and it fixes the repetition too.** Right now the prototype carries 11 near-identical urls pointing at coarse README sections (`#bot-session` covers three keys). The dedicated-file design:

- **`vc-config.md`** at the repo root: one `##` heading per key path, holding the *long-form* docs — what consumes the key, examples, rationale (col-width's 68 story would live there instead of a prototype comment). The prototype's `doc` stays the one-liner.
- **References become derived, not written**: build.rs computes `reference = <base> + "vc-config.md#" + slug(path)` for every key, with a single `reference-base` declared once at the top of the prototype (a small `[vc-config]` meta table). The 11 repeated urls disappear; a per-key override field remains for the odd key whose docs live elsewhere.
- **Drift guard**: a test parses `vc-config.md`'s headings and asserts every key's anchor exists — a key added to the prototype without docs fails the suite.
- **File-local reading falls out for free**: in this repo you open `vc-config.md` directly; the hosted url is the same file, so both audiences read one document.
- **Customization**: a fork or the family template edits `reference-base` and ships its own `vc-config.md` — that's the customization story today. A *runtime* per-workspace base override (a config key consulted at render time) is possible later, but generated files bake whatever was active when written, so I'd backlog that rather than design it now.

The base-url-in-one-place also fixes a rot vector: a repo rename currently invalidates 11 strings; with derivation it invalidates one.

The work review is open, so revising the rung now is cheap: create `vc-config.md` (seeded from the doc lines plus the col-width rationale), add the `[vc-config] reference-base` meta table, switch build.rs to derived references with optional override, add the anchor drift-guard test, and update the README subsection to match. Want me to make those changes?

input.content:
# vc-config: settable configuration keys

Long-form documentation for every settable vc-x1 config key, one section per key, headed by the
key's path. The `reference:` line in a generated config and in `vc-x1 config` output links to the
key's section here: build.rs derives the link from `[vc-config] reference-base` in
`vc-config.toml` (the schema prototype) plus the heading's anchor, and the test suite fails if a
key has no matching heading. Sections are in schema order.

The `bot-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
`.vc-config.toml`, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in
default. The other keys live in a single home each: `default.*`, `repo.*`, and `account.*` in
the user config, `repos.*` in the workspace configs.

## default.account

The account profile `init` and other account-aware commands use when `--account` is not given on
the command line: the name of an `[account.<name>]` section in the user config.

## default.debug

Reserved: the value `--debug` would assume when used without an argument. No command consumes it
yet; setting it is harmless and does nothing.

## repo.default

The repo category `--repo` assumes when given bare (no `<cat>` argument): the name of a
[repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat) entry, one of the built-ins (`remote`, `local`) or
your own.

## repo.category.\<cat\>

The literal value behind a repo category name: a remote url prefix (`init` appends
`/<NAME>.git`) or a local parent directory. `init` resolves `--repo <cat>` through this table
when its target is a path or a bare name.

## account.\<name\>.repo.default

Per-account variant of [repo.default](#repodefault): the default category used while the
`<name>` account profile is active.

## account.\<name\>.repo.category.\<cat\>

Per-account variant of [repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat): a category defined inside an
account profile, shadowing the top-level table while that account is active.

## bot-session.items

The default item set the `bot-session` conversation view renders, a comma-separated list (e.g.
`headers,user,assistant,tool,summary`). The per-item `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` flags override
individual items, and `--all` / `--none` replace the base set entirely.

## bot-session.result-lines

Maximum lines shown per tool result in the conversation view when results are rendered; `0`
means unlimited. The `--result-lines` flag overrides it.

## bot-session.col-width

# vc-config: settable configuration keys

Long-form documentation for every settable vc-x1 config key, one section per key, headed by the
key's path. The `reference:` line in a generated config and in `vc-x1 config` output links to the
key's section here: build.rs derives the link from `[vc-config] reference-base` in
`vc-config.toml` (the schema prototype) plus the heading's anchor, and the test suite fails if a
key has no matching heading. Sections are in schema order.

The `bot-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
`.vc-config.toml`, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in
default. The other keys live in a single home each: `default.*`, `repo.*`, and `account.*` in
the user config, `repos.*` in the workspace configs.

## default.account

The account profile `init` and other account-aware commands use when `--account` is not given on
the command line: the name of an `[account.<name>]` section in the user config.

## default.debug

Reserved: the value `--debug` would assume when used without an argument. No command consumes it
yet; setting it is harmless and does nothing.

## repo.default

The repo category `--repo` assumes when given bare (no `<cat>` argument): the name of a
[repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat) entry, one of the built-ins (`remote`, `local`) or
your own.

## repo.category.\<cat\>

The literal value behind a repo category name: a remote url prefix (`init` appends
`/<NAME>.git`) or a local parent directory. `init` resolves `--repo <cat>` through this table
when its target is a path or a bare name.

## account.\<name\>.repo.default

Per-account variant of [repo.default](#repodefault): the default category used while the
`<name>` account profile is active.

## account.\<name\>.repo.category.\<cat\>

Per-account variant of [repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat): a category defined inside an
account profile, shadowing the top-level table while that account is active.

## bot-session.items

The default item set the `bot-session` conversation view renders, a comma-separated list (e.g.
`headers,user,assistant,tool,summary`). The per-item `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` flags override
individual items, and `--all` / `--none` replace the base set entirely.

means unlimited. The `--result-lines` flag overrides it.

Changes made, all validated. Please review.

What changed in this revision:

- **`vc-config.md`** (new, repo root): long-form docs, one `##` section per key path — the col-width 68 rationale moved here from the prototype comment, the resolution-order story sits in the intro, and dynamic-path headings use markdown escapes (`\<cat\>`) so they render literally.
- **`vc-config.toml`**: the 11 per-key `reference` urls are gone, replaced by one `[vc-config] reference-base` meta table; `reference` remains as a documented optional override. A repo rename is now a one-line fix.
- **`build.rs`**: recognizes the `[vc-config]` meta table (required, unknown entries fail the build), and derives each reference as `reference-base + "vc-config.md#" + slug(path)` unless overridden.
- **New drift guard**: a test re-derives GitHub slugs from `vc-config.md`'s actual headings and demands every derived reference land on one — a key added to the prototype without docs fails the suite (it passed against the real file, including the escaped headings).
- **README**: the prototype subsection now tells the derived-reference story (including the fork-customization line: point `reference-base` at your repo, edit your `vc-config.md`); the three sample blocks show the real derived urls; the example key table lost its `reference` line.
- **TODO block**: the prototype rung's section updated to match (derivation bullet, vc-config.md, the new drift guard).

Validation: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, full suite (485 + integration, all green), dev binary reinstalled — so `vc-x1-dev config` now prints the derived urls if you want to click one.

One honest caveat: the derived urls point at `blob/main/vc-config.md`, which 404s until this cycle lands on `main` — inherent to hosted references, worth knowing before you click.

1	# vc-config.toml: the schema PROTOTYPE, not a config file.
2	#
3	# This file is the single source of truth for vc-x1's settable
4	# config keys. build.rs parses it and generates the schema table
5	# and default constants the binary is compiled from, so the code
6	# cannot disagree with this file. Your workspace config is
7	# `.vc-config.toml` (note the leading dot); editing THIS file
8	# changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build,
9	# and is reviewed like any source change.
10	#
11	# Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path
12	# (dynamic segments quoted: [repo.category."<cat>"]). Entries:
13	#
14	#   homes      which config file(s) accept the key: "user"
15	#              (~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml), "workspace-code",
16	#              "workspace-bot" (the two .vc-config.toml sides)
17	#   kind       value shape: "str", "usize", or "item-list"
18	#   doc        one-line description (rendered, keep it tight)
19	#   used-by    the command/flag or structural context consuming it
20	#   default    the built-in value; omit when there is none
21	#   example    representative value for keys with no default
22	#   required   active (not commented) in generated configs; the
23	#              value is role-specific, filled by init
24	#   reference  optional override url for the key's docs; when
25	#              absent (the norm) build.rs derives
26	#              <reference-base>vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>,
27	#              pointing at the key's section in vc-config.md
28	#
29	# Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream.
30

32	# settable key.

Thoughts on both — one is a clean improvement, the other needs a small build.rs change to work, with a neat resolution available.

**"Ladder details" with `#####` sections: better than my flat version.** Scanning the `####` level now shows exactly the six canonical items plus one container, instead of items interleaved with rung titles; the ladder-ToC-to-details correspondence gets a named home; and since anchors derive from heading *text*, not level, the greppability and title-identity properties survive intact. Two small notes for when the docs rung pins this: (a) at the close-out move everything shifts one level *shallower* (title `###` to `##`), so in chores the rung sections sit at `####` — comfortable; (b) under a multi-cycle *program*, the extra level puts rung sections at markdown's `######` floor while still in TODO — workable, but worth a sentence in the pinned text.

**The `reference-base` trim surfaces a real question: which ref should the url name?** Right now the join is a bare concatenation, so your edit currently produces `...vc-x1vc-config.md#...` — broken urls the drift tests don't catch (they check the fragment and the `https://`, not the middle). The fix isn't to compute the branch at build time, though — that would bake in whatever the *builder* had checked out (`config-refresh` today), pointing shipped references at a topic branch. The clean answer is GitHub's `blob/HEAD` form: `<base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor>` — `HEAD` resolves to the repo's default branch *at click time*, so nothing about branches is specified anywhere, which I think is the actual spirit of your edit: the base names the repo, full stop, and even the earlier "404s until this lands on main" caveat softens (HEAD follows whatever main becomes).

One honesty note: the `/blob/HEAD/` join is GitHub-shaped. A GitLab fork would need `/-/blob/HEAD/`; the per-key override covers the odd case, and if forks materialize, `[vc-config]` can grow a join template — I wouldn't build that speculatively.

So concretely: build.rs normalizes the base (trim any trailing `/`), joins `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<slug>`, and I'd tighten the anchor test to require `/vc-config.md#` with the slash so a bad join can't slip through again. Your prototype edit then stands as-is.

#
# This file is the single source of truth for vc-x1's settable
# config keys. build.rs parses it and generates the schema table
# and default constants the binary is compiled from, so the code
# cannot disagree with this file. Your workspace config is
# `.vc-config.toml` (note the leading dot); editing THIS file
# changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build,
# and is reviewed like any source change.
#
# Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path
# (dynamic segments quoted: [repo.category."<cat>"]). Entries:

30	This is experiment 1 to explore creating a Vibe Coding (vc) environment. We will investigate ways of
31	using the dual jj-git repo concept, explored in
32	[hw-jjg-bot](https://github.com/winksaville/hw-jjg-bot.git) to initially make it easy to see how the
33	code base evolved. This is made possible by the fact that we have two repos one with the code and
34	one with the conversation with the bot.
35	
36	I've chosen the jj-git environment because jj provides the concept that each commit has an immutable
37	changeID as well as the mutable commitID of git. The idea is that each commit made on repo A writes
38	the changeID in the commit message to repo B. Thus there is a cross reference between the two repos
39	and this will allow vc-x1 to show how the repo evolved and the entity (bot or human) can more
40	clearly understand **how** and most importantly **why** the code evolved.
41	
42	The solution space is wide open, from trivial CLI, web or app based (mobile/non-mobile). In
43	addition, I could see this as an extension to existing programming editors like vscode and zed or
44	even creating our own IDE for vc.
45	
46	See [Initial commit with dual jj-git
47	repos](./notes/chores/chores-01.md#initial-commit-with-dual-jj-git-repos) for how the initial commit
48	was created with the dual jj-git repos. After doing so and I then created this README.md file.
49	
50	## Terminology
51	
52	A vc-x1 workspace pairs two jj-git repos, and this README names their two sides **work** and
53	**bot**:
54	
55	- **work repo**: the repo at the project root, holding the work product itself (source code, docs,
56	  the repo you would have anyway).
57	- **bot repo**: the `.claude` repo nested inside it, holding the bot's session data (the
58	  conversation that produced the work).
59	- **work** / **bot**: the two sides as roles, used wherever a command or doc needs to say which repo
60	  it means (e.g. push's `commit-work` / `commit-bot` stages).
61	
62	A few naming conventions this project keeps, to avoid ambiguous jargon:
63	
64	- **path** is reserved for a filesystem location, qualified as **relative** or **absolute** when it
65	  matters (e.g. `../other`, `/home/you/repo`).
66	- a configuration setting is a **config key**, e.g. `bot-session.col-width` (its TOML table and key
67	  joined by `.`); not a "path".
68	- a datum in a transcript's `--fields` inventory is a **field**, e.g. `message.content[].type`, its
69	  levels joined by `.`, with `[]` marking array elements.
70	
71	## Build and install
72	
73	A plain Rust crate: `cargo build`, `cargo test`, and
74	
75	```
76	cargo install --path . --locked
77	```
78	
79	installs one binary named by the manifest's `[package].name`. That name is deliberate, the
80	**single-name convention** (adopted 0.78.3; design record in
81	`notes/chores/chores-16.md`):
82	
83	- On `main` the name is `vc-x1`: installing from a main-positioned tree gives you the stable
84	  binary, and that is the whole promotion ceremony.
85	- A development line renames `[package].name` to its own name (e.g. `vc-x1-dev`,
86	  `vc-x1-<topic>`) at cycle open and back to `vc-x1` at close-out, next to the version bump
87	  those steps already make. Each line's install then produces its own binary, and concurrent
88	  lines coexist on `PATH` under their own names.
89	- The guard is mechanical, not memory: `build.rs` refuses to build a tree whose version
90	  carries a dev suffix (`0.79.1-2`) while the manifest still says `vc-x1`. A build script
91	  runs on **every** cargo verb, `cargo install` included (a test would not: `cargo install`
92	  never runs tests), so a forgotten rename fails before any binary exists to clobber your

content.text:
Yes, fully agree — and I'd name the standard the docs have to meet: **a reference link must reward the click**. Right now several `vc-config.md` sections just restate the one-liner the reader was already looking at in their config file; clicking through to a paraphrase is worse than no link. The seeded file was scaffolding to make the derivation and drift test real, not finished documentation.

What "significantly improved" concretely means per section, I'd say:

- **A worked TOML example** as it would appear in the actual config file — for `repo.category.<cat>` that's a category definition *plus* the `init --repo` invocation that consumes it; for the `account.*` family, a full `[account.<name>]` profile showing the shadowing; for `bot-session.items`, a couple of named recipes (prompts-only, everything).
- **The resolution story where it's non-trivial** — the user-config account/repo chain (`default.account` -> `account.<name>.repo.default` -> `repo.category.<cat>`) is genuinely intricate and currently described one fragment per section with no overview.
- **Effects, not just meaning** — what visibly changes when the key is set (col-width got this treatment; the others didn't).

Two suggestions on top of agreeing:

1. **Give it a rung** rather than folding it into close-out — close-out is bookkeeping only by protocol, and this is real writing worth its own review. Something like `docs: vc-config.md per-key examples`, placed late (after `--refresh`, before `.agent-session`) so the examples describe the settled surface.
2. **Consider mechanizing the floor**: the anchor drift test could additionally require each key's section to contain a ` ```toml ` fence — crude, but it makes "has an example" a property the suite enforces rather than a review hope. Optional; quality itself stays a human judgment.

Want me to add the rung to the ladder (and the test-floor idea to its Ladder-details section as a decision to make when we get there)?

**Title:**

```
feat: vc-config.toml prototype + build.rs codegen
```

**Body:**

```
The settable config-key schema was hand-kept in code: a Rust table
in one file and behavioral default constants in another, with
nothing tying them together or to any documentation. The copies
could drift apart silently, and a schema entry gave a reader no
path to fuller docs than its own one-liner.

The repo-root vc-config.toml prototype is now the schema's single
source: one TOML table per settable key, parsed by build.rs, which
generates the schema table and the typed default constants the
binary compiles against. Consequences and companions:

- behavioral defaults consume the generated constants, so behavior,
  schema, and documentation cannot disagree
- every key renders a reference line, derived from one
  reference-base joined with /blob/HEAD/ and the key's heading
  anchor in the new vc-config.md, the long-form per-key docs file
- a malformed prototype fails the build, and drift-guard tests pin
  the clap help defaults, the items default against the built-in
  item set, and every derived reference to a real vc-config.md
  heading
- README documents the prototype and the derivation
```

Validation stands: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, full suite green, install done after the last code edit; the edits since were markdown-only.

Please review the description. On your go I'll push it on `config-refresh`.

175	## Chores conventions
176	
177	### Headings and entries that record a commit
178	
179	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
180	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
181	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
182	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
183	version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
184	are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
185	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
186	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
187	`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out
188	commit's title, and its shape is in [Done entry form](#done-entry-form).
189	
190	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
191	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
192	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
193	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
194	
195	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
196	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
197	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
198	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
199	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
200	
201	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
202	free-form text. The convention applies going forward.
203	
204	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
205	
206	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
207	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
208	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
209	per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
210	changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
211	body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
212	source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others; none
213	restates another.
214	
215	The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
216	`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
217	narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
218	than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
219	[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
220	two don't drift.
221	
222	**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
223	chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
224	drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.
225	
226	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
227	Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
228	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
229	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
230	direction).
231	
232	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
233	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; the body owns the problem
234	and the solution; chores owns the narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
235

239	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out
commit's title, and its shape is in [Done entry form](#done-entry-form).

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text. The convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others; none
restates another.

The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
two don't drift.

**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; the body owns the problem
and the solution; chores owns the narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.

lastPrompt: With "docs: ladder toC ..." done should we have links from the ladders to the sections?

content.text:
My recommendation is no for now, and it's worth recording why since it's a natural next thought:

- **Hand-computed slugs fail silently** — the exact failure class the four-transforms warning already names. `docs: ladder ToC + per-rung sections` slugs to `#docs-ladder-toc--per-rung-sections` (colon dropped, `+` stripped leaving a double hyphen) — easy to get wrong, and a wrong anchor renders fine and just doesn't jump. Until a `validate-repo` checks anchors, every link is an unverified liability; the chores conventions specifically flag un-checkable links as the transforms' silent failure mode.
- **The most-churned lines get the most syntax.** Rungs are edited constantly (markers flip, steps insert); wrapping each title in `[...](#...)` puts link plumbing on exactly the lines we touch most, and the title would then live twice per rung (text + slug) — the write-once principle the block was built around.
- **The navigation win is small where the links would live.** In `TODO.md` the details are one screen below the ladder; grep of the title (which stays verbatim inside link text or out) finds both instantly. And the *unlinked* asymmetry is informative as-is: you can't tell from a bare ladder which rungs have details — but that's also true with selective links, which reintroduce lumpiness.

Where links genuinely earn their keep is inbound from *other* records — a deliberation bullet, `bugs.md`, the backlog pointing at `#docs-ladder-toc--per-rung-sections` — and that works today; the headings exist for that. The rung-to-subsection hop within one block is the cheapest navigation in the file.

If tooling changes the calculus — a `validate-repo` that verifies same-file anchors — linking the ladder becomes nearly free and I'd revisit; that tool is already a known aspiration in the conventions.

Want me to add this as a considered-and-declined bullet in the rung's `Ladder details` subsection, so the question doesn't get re-litigated next cycle?

Short answer: it's designed but unscheduled — it exists whenever we give it a cycle; nothing is in flight toward it today.

The current state of the trail:

- **A full design exists** in the chores record (`vc-x1 validate-repo`, chores-06): scope, flags, per-check reporting, exit semantics, and the implementation note about promoting the `verify_*` helpers to `common.rs`.
- **Two backlog entries point at it** (#8 "Add a vc-x1 validate-repo?" and #24 with the concrete check list), so it's remembered but unranked — nothing has promoted it into `## Todo`.
- **One gap for our purpose**: the designed check list covers `[N]` reference anchors and chores-title-to-commit consistency, but *not* markdown heading anchors (the slug-computed `#docs-ladder-toc--per-rung-sections` kind the ladder links would need). That check would be an addition to the design.

Realistically, the queue ahead of it: finishing this cycle (five rungs to go), the trapezoid branch's close-out, and the two open mailbox items. So "when" is a prioritization call that's yours.

If you want it sooner, there's a cheap path: the anchor checker doesn't need the whole `validate-repo` machine. A narrow first slice — scan the notes files and README, verify every same-file `#anchor` resolves against the documented slug algorithm, plus the `[N]` refs — is a small, self-contained cycle: a markdown scanner and the slug function, no jj machinery at all. That slice alone is what flips the ladder-links calculus.

Want me to sharpen backlog #24 with the heading-anchor check and the standalone-slice note, so it's pickable in that form — or promote the slice to `## Todo` as its own ranked entry?
